text: The correct order of the complexes $[\mathrm{Co}(\mathrm{NH}_{3})_{5}(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O})]^{3+}(\mathrm{A})$, $[\mathrm{Co}(\mathrm{NH}_{3})_{6}]^{3+}(\mathrm{B})$, $[\mathrm{Co}(\mathrm{CN})_{6}]^{3-}(\mathrm{C})$ and $[\mathrm{CoCl}(\mathrm{NH}_{3})_{5}]^{2+}(\mathrm{D})$ in terms of wavelength of light absorbed is
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
All four complexes contain $\mathrm{Co}{}^{3+}$ ($3d^{6}$, low spin), and the energy of the light absorbed rises with the crystal field splitting $\Delta _{o}$; since $λ=\dfrac{hc}{E}$, a larger $\Delta _{o}$ means a shorter wavelength absorbed.

$\Delta _{o}$ follows the spectrochemical series $\mathrm{CN}{}^{-}>\mathrm{NH}{}_{3}>\mathrm{H}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}>\mathrm{Cl}{}^{-}$. Replacing one $\mathrm{NH}{}_{3}$ of $[\mathrm{Co}(\mathrm{NH}{}_{3}){}_{6}]{}^{3+}$ by $\mathrm{H}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}$ lowers $\Delta _{o}$, and replacing it by $\mathrm{Cl}{}^{-}$ lowers it further, so $\Delta _{o}$ is in the order C > B > A > D.

The wavelength of light absorbed is in the reverse order: D > A > B > C.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

text:
Which of the following statements are correct?

A. The process of adding an electron to a neutral gaseous atom is always exothermic.

B. The process of removing an electron from an isolated gaseous atom is always endothermic.

C. The $1^{\text{st}}$ ionization energy of boron is less than that of beryllium.

D. The electronegativity of C is 2.5 in $\mathrm{CH}_{4}$ and $\mathrm{CCl}_{4}$

E. Li is the most electropositive among elements of group I.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
A: Adding an electron to a neutral gaseous atom is not always exothermic; for noble gases, and for atoms such as Be and N, the electron gain enthalpy is positive. A is incorrect.

B: Removing an electron from an isolated gaseous atom always needs energy to overcome the attraction of the nucleus, so ionisation enthalpy is always positive. B is correct.

C: Be ($1s^{2}2s^{2}$) loses an electron from the filled, more penetrating $2s$ orbital, while B ($1s^{2}2s^{2}2p^{1}$) loses its single $2p$ electron, which is shielded by the $2s$ electrons; hence $IE_{1}$ of B ($801\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$) is less than that of Be ($899\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$). C is correct.

D: The electronegativity of an element is not constant; it depends on the atoms bonded to it. In $\mathrm{CCl}{}_{4}$ the four more electronegative Cl atoms leave carbon with a partial positive charge, raising its effective nuclear charge and electronegativity above that in $\mathrm{CH}{}_{4}$. D is incorrect.

E: Electropositive character increases down group 1, so Li is the least electropositive alkali metal and Cs the most. E is incorrect.

The correct statements are B and C.

Hence, the correct option is (B).

text: In the following system, $\mathrm{PCl}_{5}(\mathrm{g})⇌\mathrm{PCl}_{3}(\mathrm{g})+\mathrm{Cl}_{2}(\mathrm{g})$ at equilibrium, upon addition of xenon gas at constant $T$ and $p$, the concentration of
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Xenon is an inert gas. Adding it at constant $T$ and $p$ increases the volume, so at first $[\mathrm{PCl}{}_{5}]$, $[\mathrm{PCl}{}_{3}]$ and $[\mathrm{Cl}{}_{2}]$ all fall by the same factor.

Since two concentrations appear in the numerator and only one in the denominator, the reaction quotient

$Q_{c}=\dfrac{[\mathrm{PCl}{}_{3}][\mathrm{Cl}{}_{2}]}{[\mathrm{PCl}{}_{5}]}$

falls below $K_{c}$. The equilibrium therefore shifts forward, towards more moles of gas ($\Delta n_{g}=+1$): the amounts (moles) of $\mathrm{PCl}{}_{3}$ and $\mathrm{Cl}{}_{2}$ increase and the amount of $\mathrm{PCl}{}_{5}$ decreases.

Concentration, however, is moles per unit volume, and the shift only partly offsets the dilution. $[\mathrm{PCl}{}_{5}]$ falls, since fewer moles of it now occupy a larger volume.

If $[\mathrm{PCl}{}_{3}]$ did not fall, the reaction would have to form enough extra $\mathrm{PCl}{}_{3}$ to fill the larger volume at the old concentration. The same amount of $\mathrm{Cl}{}_{2}$ formed and of $\mathrm{PCl}{}_{5}$ used up would then make $Q_{c}>K_{c}$, which is impossible at equilibrium. Hence $[\mathrm{PCl}{}_{3}]$ decreases, and by the same argument $[\mathrm{Cl}{}_{2}]$ decreases.

Thus all three concentrations decrease; none stays constant or increases, and of the given statements only "$\mathrm{Cl}{}_{2}$ will decrease" is true.

Hence, the correct option is (C).
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift

text: Which compound would give 3-methyl-6-oxoheptanal upon ozonolysis?
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
3-Methyl-6-oxoheptanal ("oxo" is the IUPAC prefix for a ketone $\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{O}$) is $\mathrm{OHC}-\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}-\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{CH}{}_{3})-\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}-\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}-\mathrm{CO}-\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}$.

Ozonolysis of a cycloalkene cleaves the ring $\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{C}$ into a single open chain carrying both carbonyl groups, so the aldehyde carbon (C-1) and the keto carbon (C-6) were the two ends of the ring double bond.

Joining C-1 and C-6 by a double bond gives a six-membered ring with a methyl group on C-6 (from C-7) and another on C-3. C-3 and C-6 are separated by two ring carbons on each side, so the alkene is 1,4-dimethylcyclohex-1-ene, structure (A).

Ozonolysis ($\mathrm{O}{}_{3}$, then $\mathrm{Zn}/\mathrm{H}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}$) of 1,4-dimethylcyclohex-1-ene therefore gives $\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}\mathrm{CO}-\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}-\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{CH}{}_{3})-\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}-\mathrm{CHO}$.

Structures (B), (C) and (D) place the second methyl elsewhere and give 5-methyl-, 2-methyl- and 4-methyl-6-oxoheptanal respectively.

Hence, the correct option is (A).

text:
2 moles each of ethylene glycol and glucose are dissolved in 500 g of water. The boiling point of the resulting solution is:
(Given : Ebullioscopic constant of water $=0.52\mathrm{K}\mathrm{kg}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$ )
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Boiling Point Elevation Formula:

$\Delta T_{b}=i_{1}\cdot m_{1}\cdot K_{b}+i_{2}\cdot m_{2}\cdot K_{b}$

where:

$i_{1}$ and $i_{2}$ are the van't Hoff factors for ethylene glycol and glucose, respectively (both are 1 since they do not dissociate in solution).

$m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$ are the molalities of ethylene glycol and glucose, respectively.

$K_{b}$ is the ebullioscopic constant of water ($0.52\text{K kg mol}^{-1}$).

Calculate Molality:

Each solute has 2 moles dissolved in 500 grams of water ($0.5\text{kg}$):

$m_{1}=\frac{2\text{moles}}{0.5\text{kg}}=4\text{mol kg}^{-1}$

$m_{2}=\frac{2\text{moles}}{0.5\text{kg}}=4\text{mol kg}^{-1}$

Substitute into the Formula:

$\Delta T_{b}=1\cdot 4\cdot 0.52+1\cdot 4\cdot 0.52=4.16$

Determine Boiling Point of Solution:

The normal boiling point of water is $373.16\text{K}$.

Add the boiling point elevation to the normal boiling point:

$T_{b}(\text{solution})=373.16+4.16=377.3\text{K}$

Thus, the boiling point of the resulting solution is $377.3\text{K}$.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift

text:
Among $10^{-9}\mathrm{g}$ (each) of the following elements, which one will have the highest number of atoms?

Element: $\mathrm{Pb},\mathrm{Po},\mathrm{Pr}$ and Pt
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
To determine which element has the highest number of atoms among $10^{-9}$ grams of the elements Pb, Po, Pr, and Pt, we use the formula for calculating the number of atoms:

$\text{Number of atoms}=\frac{\text{Mass}}{\text{Molar Mass (g/mol)}}\times N_{A}$

where $N_{A}$ is Avogadro's number.

From this formula, it's clear that for a given mass, the element with the smallest molar mass will have the greatest number of atoms, as it appears in the denominator.

Below are the molar masses of the elements:

Molar mass of Pr (Praseodymium), $M_{\text{Pr}}=141$ g/mol

Molar mass of Pt (Platinum), $M_{\text{Pt}}=195$ g/mol

Molar mass of Pb (Lead), $M_{\text{Pb}}=207$ g/mol

Molar mass of Po (Polonium), $M_{\text{Po}}=209$ g/mol

Since Praseodymium (Pr) has the smallest molar mass ($M_{\text{Pr}}=141$ g/mol$), 10^{-9}$ grams of Pr will contain the highest number of atoms compared to the other elements listed.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift

text:
The metal ions that have the calculated spin-only magnetic moment value of 4.9 B.M. are :

A. $\mathrm{Cr}^{2+}$

B. $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$

C. $\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}$

D. $\mathrm{Co}^{2+}$

E. $\mathrm{Mn}^{3+}$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For spin-only moment, $μ=\sqrt{n(n+2)}\text{BM}$; $μ=4.9$ BM gives $n(n+2)=24$, so $n=4$ unpaired electrons.

$\mathrm{Cr}$ ($Z=24$) is $[\mathrm{Ar}]3d^{5}4s^{1}$; $\mathrm{Cr}{}^{2+}$ loses the $4s$ electron and one $3d$ electron, giving $3d^{4}$ with 4 unpaired electrons.

$\mathrm{Fe}{}^{2+}$ ($Z=26$) is $3d^{6}$: 4 unpaired. $\mathrm{Fe}{}^{3+}$ is $3d^{5}$: 5 unpaired ($μ=5.92$ BM).

$\mathrm{Co}{}^{2+}$ ($Z=27$) is $3d^{7}$: 3 unpaired ($μ=3.87$ BM). $\mathrm{Mn}{}^{3+}$ ($Z=25$) is $3d^{4}$: 4 unpaired.

The ions with $μ=4.9$ BM are A ($\mathrm{Cr}{}^{2+}$), B ($\mathrm{Fe}{}^{2+}$) and E ($\mathrm{Mn}{}^{3+}$).

Hence, the correct option is (B).

text:
Given below are two statements :

Statement I : A catalyst cannot alter the equilibrium constant $(\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{c}})$ of the reaction, temperature remaining constant.

Statement II : A homogeneous catalyst can change the equilibrium composition of a system, temperature remaining constant.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below
options: Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Let's analyze both statements:

Statement I: "A catalyst cannot alter the equilibrium constant ($K_{c}$) of the reaction, temperature remaining constant."  

A catalyst speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions equally, allowing the system to reach equilibrium faster.  

However, it does not change the energy difference between reactants and products (i.e., the Gibbs free energy change), which directly determines the equilibrium constant.  

Therefore, this statement is true.

Statement II: "A homogeneous catalyst can change the equilibrium composition of a system, temperature remaining constant."  

A homogeneous catalyst acts in the same phase as the reactants and, like any catalyst, it only helps the reaction reach equilibrium more quickly.  

It does not alter the equilibrium position, meaning the relative concentrations of reactants and products at equilibrium remain unchanged if the temperature is constant.  

Thus, this statement is false.

In summary:

Statement I is true.

Statement II is false.

The correct answer is: Option A.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift

text: Correct order of limiting molar conductivity for cations in water at 298 K is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Limiting molar conductivities in water at 298 K (in $\text{S cm}^{2}\text{mol}^{-1}$): $\mathrm{H}{}^{+}$ 349.6, $\mathrm{Ca}{}^{2+}$ 119.0, $\mathrm{Mg}{}^{2+}$ 106.0, $\mathrm{K}{}^{+}$ 73.5, $\mathrm{Na}{}^{+}$ 50.1.

$\mathrm{H}{}^{+}$ is the highest because it moves by proton transfer along hydrogen-bonded water molecules (Grotthuss mechanism) instead of migrating as a whole hydrated ion.

$\mathrm{Ca}{}^{2+}$ and $\mathrm{Mg}{}^{2+}$ exceed $\mathrm{K}{}^{+}$ and $\mathrm{Na}{}^{+}$ because one mole of a divalent ion carries two moles of charge, which raises its molar conductivity.

Within each pair the smaller ion has the higher charge density, is more heavily hydrated and so moves more slowly, giving $\mathrm{Ca}{}^{2+}>\mathrm{Mg}{}^{2+}$ and $\mathrm{K}{}^{+}>\mathrm{Na}{}^{+}$.

$\mathrm{H}{}^{+}>\mathrm{Ca}{}^{2+}>\mathrm{Mg}{}^{2+}>\mathrm{K}{}^{+}>\mathrm{Na}{}^{+}$

Hence, the correct option is (B).

text: In a reaction $A+B\to C$, initial concentrations of $A$ and $B$ are related as $[A]_{0}=8[B]_{0}$. The half lives of $A$ and $B$ are 10 min and 40 min , respectively. If they start to disappear at the same time, both following first order kinetics, after how much time will the concentration of both the reactants be same?
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The initial conditions are:

$[A]_{0}=8[B]_{0}$

Half-life of A, $\left [\text{t}_{1/2}\right ]_{A}=10\text{\min }$

Half-life of B, $\left [\text{t}_{1/2}\right ]_{B}=40\text{\min }$

Both reactants follow first-order kinetics, and we want to find the time, $t$, when $[A]_{t}=[B]_{t}$.

Step-by-step Derivation:

Write the First-order Rate Equation:

For first-order reactions, the concentration $[X]_{t}$ at time $t$ is given by:

$[X]_{t}=[X]_{0}e^{-k_{X}t}$

where $k_{X}$ is the rate constant for substance $X$.

Express Half-life through Rate Constant:

For first-order reactions, the rate constant $k$ is related to the half-life $\text{t}_{1/2}$ by:

$k=\frac{\ln 2}{\text{t}_{1/2}}$

Substituting the known half-lives:

$k_{A}=\frac{\ln 2}{10}$

$k_{B}=\frac{\ln 2}{40}$

Set Up the Equality from the Condition $[A]_{t}=[B]_{t}$:

$[A]_{0}e^{-k_{A}t}=[B]_{0}e^{-k_{B}t}$

By inserting the initial condition $[A]_{0}=8[B]_{0}$, it becomes:

$8[B]_{0}e^{-k_{A}t}=[B]_{0}e^{-k_{B}t}$

Simplify and Solve for $t$:

Divide both sides by $[B]_{0}$:

$8e^{-k_{A}t}=e^{-k_{B}t}$

Taking the natural logarithm of both sides:

$\ln 8=k_{A}t-k_{B}t$

Replace $k_{A}$ and $k_{B}$ with their expressions:

$\ln 8=\left (\frac{\ln 2}{10}-\frac{\ln 2}{40}\right )t$

Simplify Further:

$\ln 8=\ln 2\left (\frac{1}{10}-\frac{1}{40}\right )t$

Simplify $\left (\frac{1}{10}-\frac{1}{40}\right )$ to get:

$\frac{1}{10}-\frac{1}{40}=\frac{4-1}{40}=\frac{3}{40}$

So,

$\ln 8=\ln 2\times \frac{3}{40}\times t$

Final Expression for $t$:

$t=\frac{\ln 8}{\ln 2\times \frac{3}{40}}$

Calculate the value of $t$ using $\ln 8=3\ln 2$:

$t=\frac{3\ln 2}{\ln 2\times \frac{3}{40}}=\frac{40}{1}=40\text{\min }$

Therefore, after 40 minutes, the concentration of both reactants A and B will be the same.

text:
Number of molecules from below which cannot give iodoform reaction is :

Ethanol, Isopropyl alcohol, Bromoacetone, 2-Butanol, 2-Butanone, Butanal, 2-Pentanone, 3-Pentanone, Pentanal and 3-Pentanol.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The iodoform reaction is given by compounds containing the $\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}\mathrm{CO}{}^{-}$ group (and ethanal) and by alcohols containing $\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{OH}){}^{-}$ (and ethanol), which $\mathrm{I}{}_{2}$/NaOH oxidises to such carbonyl compounds.

Positive: ethanol $\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}\mathrm{OH}$, isopropyl alcohol $\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{OH})\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}$, bromoacetone $\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}\mathrm{COCH}{}_{2}\mathrm{Br}$, 2-butanol $\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{OH})\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}$, 2-butanone $\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}\mathrm{COCH}{}_{2}\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}$ and 2-pentanone $\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}\mathrm{COCH}{}_{2}\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}$.

Negative: butanal $\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}\mathrm{CHO}$ and pentanal $\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}(\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}){}_{3}\mathrm{CHO}$ (aldehydes other than ethanal), 3-pentanone $\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}\mathrm{COCH}{}_{2}\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}$ and 3-pentanol $\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{OH})\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}$ (ethyl groups on both sides of the functional carbon).

Number of compounds that cannot give the iodoform reaction $=4$.

Hence, the correct option is (A).
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift

text:
Consider the following reactions

$\begin{array}{l} \mathrm{A}+\mathrm{NaCl}_{\begin{array}{l} \text{Little} \\ \text{amount} \end{array}}+\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{SO}_{4}\to \mathrm{CrO}_{2}\mathrm{Cl}_{2}+\text{Side Products} \\ \mathrm{CrO}_{2}\mathrm{Cl}_{2\text{(Vapour)}}+\mathrm{NaOH}\to \mathrm{B}+\mathrm{NaCl}+\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O} \\ \mathrm{B}+\mathrm{H}^{+}\to \mathrm{C}+\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O} \end{array}$

The number of terminal ' $O$ ' present in the compound $' C ' is__________$
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Chromyl chloride test: a dichromate heated with a chloride and concentrated sulphuric acid gives orange-red vapours of $\mathrm{CrO}{}_{2}\mathrm{Cl}{}_{2}$, so A is $\mathrm{K}{}_{2}\mathrm{Cr}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}{}_{7}$.

$\mathrm{K}{}_{2}\mathrm{Cr}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}{}_{7}+4\mathrm{NaCl}+6\mathrm{H}{}_{2}\mathrm{SO}{}_{4}\longrightarrow 2\mathrm{CrO}{}_{2}\mathrm{Cl}{}_{2}+2\mathrm{KHSO}{}_{4}+4\mathrm{NaHSO}{}_{4}+3\mathrm{H}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}$

The vapours absorbed in $\mathrm{NaOH}$ give yellow sodium chromate, so B is $\mathrm{Na}{}_{2}\mathrm{CrO}{}_{4}$.

$\mathrm{CrO}{}_{2}\mathrm{Cl}{}_{2}+4\mathrm{NaOH}\longrightarrow \mathrm{Na}{}_{2}\mathrm{CrO}{}_{4}+2\mathrm{NaCl}+2\mathrm{H}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}$

On acidification chromate changes to dichromate, so C is $\mathrm{Na}{}_{2}\mathrm{Cr}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}{}_{7}$.

$2~\mathrm{CrO}{}_{4}{}^{2-}+2\mathrm{H}{}^{+}\longrightarrow \mathrm{Cr}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}{}_{7}{}^{2-}+\mathrm{H}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}$

In $\mathrm{Cr}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}{}_{7}{}^{2-}$ two $\mathrm{CrO}{}_{4}$ tetrahedra share one corner, so one O bridges the two Cr atoms and each Cr carries three terminal O atoms: $7-1=6$ terminal O.


[IMG]

Hence, the answer is 6.

text:
0.5 g of an organic compound on combustion gave 1.46 g of $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ and 0.9 g of $\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$. The percentage of carbon in the compound is $_______________. ($Nearest integer)

[Given : Molar mass (in $\left. \mathrm{g}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}\right )\mathrm{C}:12,\mathrm{H}:1,\mathrm{O}:16$ ]
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
To determine the percentage of carbon in the organic compound, follow these steps:

Calculate Moles of CO₂:

Given: 1.46 g of CO₂ is produced.

Molar mass of CO₂ = 44 g/mol.

Moles of CO₂ = $\frac{1.46\text{g}}{44\text{g/mol}}$.

Determine Moles of Carbon Atoms:

Each molecule of CO₂ contains one atom of carbon.

Thus, moles of carbon = moles of CO₂.

Calculate Mass of Carbon:

Molar mass of carbon (C) = 12 g/mol.

Mass of carbon = Moles of carbon × 12 g/mol.

Mass of carbon = $\frac{1.46}{44}\times 12$.

Calculate Percentage of Carbon:

Total mass of the organic compound = 0.5 g.

Percentage of carbon = $\left (\frac{\text{Mass of carbon}}{0.5\text{g}}\right )\times 100%$.

Hence, Percentage of carbon = $\frac{1.46}{44}\times \frac{12}{0.5}\times 100$.

Percentage of carbon = 79.63%.

Therefore, the percentage of carbon in the compound is approximately 80%.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift

text:
The number of optical isomers exhibited by the iron complex $(\mathrm{A})$ obtained from the following reaction $is___________$.

$\mathrm{FeCl}_{3}+\mathrm{KOH}+\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{C}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{4}\to \mathrm{A}$
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Oxalic acid neutralised by KOH supplies oxalate ions, which replace chloride around $\mathrm{Fe}{}^{3+}$:

$\mathrm{FeCl}{}_{3}+6\mathrm{KOH}+3\mathrm{H}{}_{2}\mathrm{C}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}{}_{4}\longrightarrow \mathrm{K}{}_{3}[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{C}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}{}_{4}){}_{3}]+3\mathrm{KCl}+6\mathrm{H}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}$

The complex ion $[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{C}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}{}_{4}){}_{3}]{}^{3-}$ in A is an octahedral $[\mathrm{M}(\mathrm{AA})_{3}]$ complex with three bidentate oxalate ligands.

An $[\mathrm{M}(\mathrm{AA})_{3}]$ complex has no geometrical isomers, but its propeller-like arrangement of three chelate rings is chiral and exists as two non-superimposable mirror images, the $\Delta$ and $\Lambda$ forms.

Hence, the answer is 2.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 3rd April Morning Shift
